mcqs.question: Why does ShortenerService depend on Encoder and Repository as interfaces rather than concrete classes?
options: Interfaces are required by the language and provide no design benefit here
Because a Repository cannot store more than one type of object otherwise
Because UrlMapping objects are immutable and require an interface to be constructed
So the encoding scheme and the storage mechanism can each be swapped independently without changing the other or the service that composes them
mcqs.explanation: Depending on interfaces is what lets encoding and storage vary independently — swap a Base62CounterEncoder for a HashEncoder, or an in-memory Repository for a real database, without touching ShortenerService or each other. This isn't a language requirement, has nothing to do with a Repository's type capacity, and UrlMapping's immutability is unrelated to interface use here.

mcqs.question: What is the fundamental trade-off between a base62-counter encoder and a hash-truncation encoder?
options: The counter guarantees no collisions but needs a coordinated shared counter source; hash truncation needs no coordination but can collide and requires explicit handling
The counter approach is always slower to compute than hashing
Hash truncation can never produce a code shorter than 32 characters
The counter approach cannot be used with a base62 alphabet
mcqs.explanation: The core trade-off is coordination versus collision risk: a counter is collision-free by construction but requires a single shared source of truth, while hashing avoids that coordination cost at the price of needing a collision-retry path. Counter encoding isn't inherently slower, hash truncation can be any length you choose, and base62 is exactly the encoding a counter typically uses.

mcqs.question: Which encoding approach is the only one of the three where the same input URL always produces the same short code, with no lookup-first check needed to keep it that way?
options: All three always produce the same code for the same URL
mcqs.explanation: Hashing is deterministic on its input, so the same URL naturally maps to the same code without any extra bookkeeping. A counter advances on every call regardless of input, and random-then-check picks a fresh random code each time by design — neither is naturally deterministic per URL.
